realLife: Mixtures model customer behaviour groups, speaker voices and background in video, wherever groups overlap and a soft label is more honest than a hard one.
summary: Model the data as a blend of bell-shaped groups and let each point belong to several at once.
headline: Soft clusters with their own shapes
overview: A Gaussian mixture says the data came from several bell-shaped clumps. Each point gets a probability of belonging to each one, instead of a single hard label.

The expectation-maximisation loop alternates between guessing those probabilities and refitting each bell. You choose how flexible each bell is: a circle, a stretched axis-aligned ellipse, or a freely tilted ellipse.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Give blobs 7 free-tilting components. Log-likelihood keeps climbing as the fit improves, yet BIC turns upward because extra parameters cost more than they gain.

check.question: Why look at BIC instead of log-likelihood to choose the number of components?
options: Likelihood always improves with more components, BIC charges for the extra parameters

data: Blobs, unequal blobs and stretched blobs, fitted with 1 to 7 components in three covariance shapes. Starting means come from k-means. The engine matches scikit-learn's likelihood, BIC and means from the same start.
maths: p counts free parameters. A small value is added to each covariance diagonal so a component cannot collapse onto a single point.
code:
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
m = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, covariance_type='full', random_state=0).fit(X)
m.bic(X), m.predict_proba(X)
